extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in oral tradition, folklore, and historiography
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing methodological principles, definitions, and practical guidance for studying, collecting, and evaluating oral traditions across cultures, with attention to formulaic composition, fieldwork, chronology, and interpretive frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral-formulaic composition / formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Large amounts of 'formulaic' phraseology (oral formulas) appear in oral corpora; in the Quran many repeated phrases and attributes (e.g., 'Allah created the heavens and the earth') are examples of these formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat frequent, repeated multi-word phrases as evidence of oral-formulaic composition; quantitative estimates (e.g., up to one third of the Quran) and computational analysis of lexical repetition (Bannister) can corroborate oral transmission. Beware narrow 'verbatim' definitions of formula — generative-template models (Fry) allow variation within metrical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vansina's working definition of oral tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral tradition as 'oral statements spoken, sung or called out on musical instruments only' and requiring 'transmission by word of mouth over at least a generation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this historian-oriented working definition for evaluating oral materials as historical sources, while recognizing that sociologists, linguists, and folklorists may adopt different definitions emphasizing common knowledge, linguistic features, or artistic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of oral traditions as historical sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral traditions can be valid sources for reconstructing the past (Jan Vansina's argument) and have been used in African historiography and other areas where written sources are scarce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate oral evidence with auxiliary disciplines (archaeology, linguistics) and contemporary written records when available; treat oral material as potentially informative but require careful method and critical evaluation of reliability, provenance, and changes over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fieldwork collection best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Fieldwork and transcription are primary methods to collect oral traditions, but early practices often failed to archive tapes or used non-fluent researchers and interpreters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer audio (or video) recordings over plain transcriptions because tapes capture attitudes, laughter, hesitations, and performance cues. Deposit recordings in public depositories for verifiability. Use fluent native-language researchers or collaborate closely with emic (insider) informants; avoid overreliance on interpreters who may distort meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewing format: individual vs group
rubrics_metrics.description: Individualised interviews tend to be preferred because group performances involve narrator and audience shaping the story and may prioritise improvisation for entertainment over factual accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the research goal is accuracy of events or tracing historical content, prioritise individual accounts; when studying performance dynamics or communal meaning, group settings are informative. Note that group dynamics can introduce improvisation and feedback from written sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronology and dating via generational averaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Because oral tradition rarely incorporates chronological devices, historians often use 'generational averaging' to establish dates and chronologies; a common length chosen for generations is 27 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lists of rulers and generational averaging cautiously; cross-check with contemporary written sources when possible. Be alert for lists that grow over time or for other signs that may harm chronological credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance-centred interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaning in oral traditions often 'sits in the performance' rather than being fully captured by transcription; oral traditions enact struggles, power relations, and speaker-audience dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give analytic weight to performance context, the storyteller's agency and biography, audience interaction, and non-verbal cues. Avoid relying solely on text transcripts for interpretation; consider ethnographic and performative data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mnemonic core images / clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral historians reconstruct traditions through mnemonic systems; scholars call the central elements 'core images' or 'clichés' which are key to historical interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify recurring core images as anchors of memory and meaning; use them to trace lineage, variation, and cultural emphases across versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulaic system with substitution slots
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'formulaic system' concept includes structural 'substitution slots' allowing syntactic, morphological and narrative necessity alongside artistic invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model formulas as templates permitting variation in word choice and form. Use such models to reconcile apparent repetition with room for creativity and to analyse constraints imposed by meter or performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-level formulaic patterns (ring composition, type-scene, responsion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale structural features—'ring composition', 'responsion', and 'type-scene' (or 'theme')—and characteristic patterns (e.g., 'Beasts of Battle', 'Cliffs of Death', 'arming sequence', 'hero on the beach') organize oral narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for recurring narrative scenes and structural schemas that govern episode order and detail distribution; these patterns can have broad geographic distribution and inform comparative analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary vs secondary orality descriptors (Ong)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish 'primary orality' (cultures untouched by writing) from 'secondary orality' (electronic-age orality sustained by writing/print); Ong provides descriptors used to index the relative orality or literacy of texts or societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the psychodynamics/descriptor set to classify texts and cultures along an orality-literacy spectrum; recognise that most contemporary societies show mixed features rather than pure primary orality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-formulaic hybrid recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Some written works demonstrate 'written-formulaic' status: while demonstrably written, they contain evidence of oral influences, like heavy reliance on formulas and themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a rigid oral/literate binary; analyse written texts for oral-derived formulas, themes, and placement rules (e.g., Anglo-Saxon poetry). Treat hybridity as an analytic possibility rather than anomaly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing authorship and performer agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Debates about oral tradition often hinge on how much creativity and intellectual authorship to attribute to individual reciters versus seeing texts as collective repertoires or 'reproductive'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing authorship or creativity, consider metrical constraints, the reciter's role, cultural norms of performance, and comparative differences between traditions (e.g., Serbo-Croatian vs Homeric practices). Do not assume formulaic patterns negate creative agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological interdisciplinary scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The methodology of oral tradition conditions studies across folklore, literature, literacy studies, philosophy, communication theory, semiotics, biblical studies and more, and now informs hermeneutics and aesthetics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt interdisciplinary tools (hermeneutics, semiotics, performance studies) for richer interpretation; be explicit about theoretical frame and its implications for data collection and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archival and verifiability concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Many early field collections failed to deposit tapes and transcriptions in public depositories, harming verifiability and future critique of interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure proper archival of primary recordings and metadata; document provenance, informants, recording conditions, and any translation procedures to support future verification and reanalysis.
